text: A role is a record on sys_user_role. On its own it's barely more than a name — its real power comes from everything else in the platform configured to check for it: ACLs, UI actions, menu visibility. A group is about who's on a team; a role is about what a user is actually permitted to do.

Role assignment lives in sys_user_has_role, tracking which user holds which role. You assign it from the user's Roles related list, or from the Role record's list of users. Common roles you'll use constantly: itil for baseline agent access, itil_admin for ITIL configuration, and admin for essentially everything.

Here's the mechanism that makes this powerful and risky: a role's Contains Roles related list. If Role A contains Role B, anyone with Role A automatically has every permission Role B grants too — real inheritance, resolved by the platform, not just a label.

Two examples to know cold. The admin role contains nearly every other role — granting admin is never just one role. And itil_admin contains itil, so an ITIL admin automatically gets base ITIL permissions without a separate assignment.

Because of inheritance, you can never answer what can this user do by looking only at the roles on their record — you have to check what each role contains too. Before granting any unfamiliar role, open its Contains Roles list first. That habit is the everyday face of least privilege.

Roles decide what a user can actually do, and containment means one grant can quietly become several. Next up: delegated administration — giving someone scoped admin power without handing them full admin.
